<reason>A made the decisive distinction between tourism’s geographic share and its actual intensity: enforceable caps can relieve overload without expanding the visitor footprint. B offered plausible benefits from secondary attractions and steadier employment, but repeatedly treated regulated concentration as necessarily destructive while assuming regulation would protect newly promoted neighborhoods. A answered both pressure questions directly and developed the stronger comparison of marginal relief against additional disruption and servicing costs. B’s concession that shoulder-season growth is not necessarily redistribution also left its seasonal case insufficiently resolved.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s strongest rebuttal was that a high share of a smaller, controlled total need not constitute a crush. This directly defeated B’s repeated claim that unchanged itineraries prevent relief, while A’s equal-safeguards challenge exposed the inconsistent treatment of housing rules and caps across the two policies.</best_rebuttal>
